pitfalls: Letters say 'repeat bloods' without a date → count only a date or a time frame as a pass.
Stage 1 AKI would swamp the sample → restrict to stage 2–3 and keep the same rule in cycle 2.
The trigger fires for patients who died or were transferred → exclude them in both cycles.
GPs receive the date but no one books the test → add a line asking the patient to book it, and ask the GP forum for feedback.
pearls: Recruit the EPR team early; the trigger is the hard part.
Agree default time frames with the renal team (e.g. 1–2 weeks for stage 3).
Invite a GP to the presentation; they will champion the change.
Use the lab AKI alert list for cases: it is complete and time-stamped.

pitfalls: ECG done but not time-stamped in the notes → use the ECG machine or ECG system time.
Pseudo-hyperkalaemia from haemolysed samples → exclude only if the report or repeat confirms it.
Nurses unsure whether they may record an ECG without a doctor → agree before cycle 1 that the ECG is a nurse-initiated step.
Out-of-hours delays → report day and night separately.
pearls: Recruit the biochemistry duty lead; the critical-results log gives every case.
Agree a nurse-initiated ECG policy with nursing leadership.
Keep an ECG machine on each acute ward charged and stocked.
Use the same ECG for the calcium decision and write the finding in one line.

pitfalls: Blood-gas potassium not in the EPR → agree before cycle 1 how to retrieve analyser results and search both.
Treatment time unclear → use the administration time on the drug chart, not the prescription time.
Patients moved from ED to a ward mid-treatment → follow the patient, not the location.
Staff treat the 2-hour check as the last one → also record the 4–6 hour check as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the point-of-care testing lead to help pull blood-gas data.
Put the recheck times on the prescription so nurses can act without a doctor.
Combine the timed potassium and glucose checks on one hyperkalaemia chart.
Present rebound cases as short stories; they persuade better than percentages.

pitfalls: Identifying treated patients is hard → use pharmacy issues of potassium binders and insulin-glucose order sets, not coding.
'Bloods with GP' written with no date → count only a date or a time frame.
Hospital clinic follow-up without bloods → check the clinic letter or booking before counting as a pass.
Readmission numbers are small → report them as context, not as the pass measure.
pearls: Recruit the renal pharmacist; they already track binder use.
Link the trigger to the same order set used for treatment.
Suggest default time frames (e.g. within 1 week if a RAAS drug is restarted).
Tell the GP which drugs were stopped or changed in the same section.

pitfalls: Late referrals from primary care inflate catheter starts → the 90-day rule excludes true late presenters; keep it for both cycles.
Fistula created but not mature → record the reason; it points to surgical waiting times, not referral.
Small numbers per quarter → use 12 months for cycle 1 and 6 months for cycle 2, and report counts with percentages.
Surgeons see the audit as blame → co-present with them and focus on the referral step.
pearls: Recruit the vascular access nurse; they hold most of the dates.
Agree the eGFR trigger with the low-clearance clinic lead before cycle 1.
Track time from referral to surgery as a secondary measure.
Share each catheter start at MDT as a short case review.

pitfalls: Glucose readings recorded on paper and in the meter but not the EPR → agree before cycle 1 which source is used and keep it.
10% glucose prescribed but not hung → use the fluid chart start time, not the prescription.
Small numbers of DKA → extend the look-back to 12 months and keep the window the same in cycle 2.
Nurses unsure they can start a pre-prescribed fluid → get nursing policy sign-off before the change.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse as co-lead.
Put the 14 mmol/L trigger in bold on the hourly monitoring chart.
Count hypoglycaemia during treatment; it shows why the step matters.
Brief ED and AMU nurse leads, as most delays happen at handover.

pitfalls: Friday and weekend admissions fail by design → report weekday and weekend separately, and agree how 'working day' is counted before cycle 1.
Reviews not written in the main notes → search the diabetes team's own system too.
Referral happens but review is by phone → count only a face-to-face or documented virtual review.
Short stays discharged before review → record them and give them a follow-up call as part of the fix.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient lead nurse; they can report their referral log.
Build the referral into the fixed-rate insulin order so it cannot be missed.
Show readmission data to support a business case for weekend cover.
Keep the same working-day rule in both cycles.

pitfalls: HHS miscoded as DKA or hyperglycaemia → search both codes and the diabetes team log.
Small numbers → use 12–24 months of cases and report counts, not only percentages.
Senior clinicians start insulin for good reasons (e.g. ketones rising during fluid treatment) → accept a documented senior reason as a pass and report it.
Calculated osmolality not recorded → calculate it from the results as (2×Na) + glucose + urea.
pearls: Recruit a diabetes consultant and the ED lead nurse.
Put the HHS pathway next to the DKA pathway in ED so the right one is picked.
Include an osmolality calculator on the chart.
Review every HHS case at the diabetes team meeting for the first 6 months.

pitfalls: LMWH withheld because of AKI → use renal-adjusted dosing, not omission; record the eGFR.
Given the next evening after a late admission → measure from admission time, not the date.
Small numbers → report counts with percentages and extend the look-back if needed.
Generic VTE assessment scores HHS as low risk → the order set should override the generic tool.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation pharmacist.
Pair this with the HHS insulin-timing audit and one HHS pathway.
Add 'daily foot check' to the same order set; HHS patients are also at high risk of heel ulcers.
Share any VTE events as case stories.

pitfalls: Some Trusts allow nurses to give glucose under a patient group direction → record this and agree before cycle 1 whether it counts as a pass.
Order sets create alert fatigue → keep the rescue items quiet (pre-selected, no pop-up).
Point-prevalence results vary by ward → sweep the same wards in both cycles.
Glucagon stocks short on some wards → check ward stock alongside prescribing.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse and the medicines safety pharmacist.
Link the rescue items to the insulin prescription itself.
Check that each ward has an in-date hypo box on the same day.
Report results by ward on one slide; wards compete to improve.

pitfalls: Readings below 3.0 from poor technique → exclude only if a repeat within 5 minutes was normal and documented.
Reviews that say 'noted' without a dose decision → count only reviews that state cause and decision.
DISN notes held in a separate system → search it and agree access before cycle 1.
Workload fears from the diabetes team → estimate weekly numbers from cycle 1 before switching on the referral.
pearls: Recruit the point-of-care testing manager; the glucose system already holds every reading.
Ask the DISN team to co-own the referral rule.
Track repeat hypos within 48 hours; it shows the benefit quickly.
Add the review to the ward's morning huddle list.

pitfalls: Risk criteria assessed after feeding starts → use the dietetic assessment and admission data to judge risk as it was on the start day.
Thiamine prescribed but not given because the patient is nil by mouth → allow IV vitamin B preparation and count administration, not prescription.
Feed started out of hours before dietetic review → report out-of-hours starts separately.
Doctors assume the dietitian prescribes → agree before cycle 1 who prescribes (usually the medical team on dietetic advice).
pearls: Recruit a nutrition support dietitian and the nutrition nurse as co-leads.
Put the risk criteria as tick boxes on the feed prescription, not in a separate document.
Add the same prompt to the out-of-hours NG feeding protocol.
Report phosphate falls; they make the risk real to ward teams.

pitfalls: Cardiologists may work out the score but not write it down → count only a recorded score, and agree this rule before cycle 1 so the baseline is not disputed.
The diagnosis time is unclear when troponin rises late → use the first note that states NSTEMI or unstable angina, and keep the same rule in both cycles.
Type 2 myocardial infarction coded as NSTEMI inflates the denominator → exclude cases relabelled by cardiology in the discharge diagnosis.
Staff see the score as paperwork → show the link between score, 72-hour angiography decision and length of stay when presenting.
The field is skipped at night → check completion on the next morning's board round for the first 4 weeks.
pearls: Recruit the MINAP data clerk; the extract gives the case list in minutes.
Agree with cardiology which scores count before cycle 1 (GRACE 6-month mortality is the default).
Put the calculator link in the proforma so the score takes under a minute.
Ask the chest pain or cardiology nurse to own the field so it survives trainee rotation.

pitfalls: Transferred patients are hard to trace → use the MINAP record, which follows the patient, or the tertiary centre's discharge letter.
Clock start differs between hospitals → use first admission time, as NICE does, in both cycles.
Frail patients managed medically lower the rate → exclude those with a documented contraindication or informed refusal, and report them separately.
Delays sit in the PCI centre's bed capacity → record the reason for each delay so the change targets the right step, and invite the PCI centre lead from the start.
pearls: Recruit the MINAP lead and the cardiac network manager before cycle 1.
Split results by weekday and weekend admission; weekend referrals often explain most breaches.
Agree the referral route with the PCI centre before changing it.
Keep the 'awaiting angiography' list on the board-round agenda so it outlives the audit team.

pitfalls: The laboratory may reject HbA1c added to every ACS panel → agree the order set with the biochemistry lead before cycle 1.
Point-of-care glucose values are missed → search both laboratory and point-of-care results for the glucose threshold.
Known diabetes is not recorded in hospital notes → check the GP summary care record before excluding.
An HbA1c is done but nobody acts on a high result → record the action field so the next step can be fixed if needed.
pearls: Recruit a biochemist and the cardiology pharmacist early.
Fix the glucose threshold (above 11.0 mmol/L) before cycle 1 and keep it.
An order-set change is cheap and lasts after trainees rotate.
Share the number of new diabetes diagnoses found; it keeps the change supported.

pitfalls: Advice given by phone is not written down → count a dated advice note in the EPR, and agree this before cycle 1.
The heart failure team may fear more referrals than they can see → agree a threshold and triage rule with them before switching on the alert.
Short stays are discharged before review → report stays under 48 hours separately.
Coded diagnoses miss patients admitted with 'breathlessness' → cross-check the NICOR list against the NT-proBNP list.
pearls: Recruit the heart failure specialist nurse lead as co-author from the start.
The laboratory can usually build the NT-proBNP alert in a few weeks; ask early.
Report results by admitting ward so wards can see their own gap.
Hand the monthly figure to the heart failure team so it outlasts the audit team.

pitfalls: Echo capacity is the real limit → involve the echo lead before cycle 1 and measure request-to-report time as well.
NICE says 'consider' → present this as a local standard supported by NICE, not a mandate.
Patients with an old echo are counted wrongly → check the echo system for any study in the last 6 months.
Weekend admissions breach most → report weekday and weekend results separately.
pearls: Recruit the chief cardiac physiologist; they know where the slots can come from.
Use the laboratory natriuretic peptide list to find cases quickly.
Agree the peptide thresholds before cycle 1.
Link the slot to the heart failure team review so one referral does both.

pitfalls: Scales are missing or broken → check scale availability on each ward before cycle 1.
Weights are written on paper and not in the EPR → agree one place to look and keep it for both cycles.
Bed-bound patients cannot be weighed → count a documented reason as an exclusion, not a fail.
Nurses feel blamed → present the results by ward system, not by individual.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister from each main medical ward.
Report day-level and patient-level results; day-level shows progress sooner.
Ask the EPR team for the diuretic-linked task early; it is a small build.
Add a weigh-in time to the morning routine so it becomes habit.

pitfalls: Red flags are not recorded, so eligible patients cannot be found → also count patients with no red flag assessment and report them.
Discharged patients' referrals are reviewed days later → record the review time from the referral system, not the referral time.
Cardiology may worry about extra referrals → share the red flag list and expected numbers before switching on the referral.
Coding misses 'fall' presentations that were blackouts → search free text for 'collapse' and 'blackout' too.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a cardiology registrar as joint leads.
Agree what 'reviewed' means (triage decision recorded) before cycle 1.
Report older adults without prodrome separately; NICE says consider referral for them too.
Keep the proforma in the ED EPR so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Blood gas times on paper differ from the analyser → use the analyser time for both cycles.
The qualifying gas is unclear when several are taken → take the gas recorded as prompting the decision; if none, the first acidotic gas after medical treatment.
Teaching alone made delays worse in one hospital → pick a system change, not another e-learning module.
Small monthly numbers swing the rate → use at least 40 episodes and report the median minutes as well.
pearls: Recruit the NIV lead nurse and an ED consultant from the start.
Map the steps from gas to mask on one real case before cycle 1; it shows where time goes.
Record the delay reason every time; it tells you what to fix.
Report door-to-mask time to the NIV group monthly so it lasts after the audit.

pitfalls: Plans are written but not timed → accept the note time in the EPR, and agree this before cycle 1.
Juniors feel unable to set a ceiling at night → allow a registrar plan 'for review by consultant' to pass, and record the grade.
A general TEP form exists but is not NIV-specific → count it if it states the ventilation ceiling clearly.
Staff may object that plans delay NIV → make the box a single line so it takes under a minute.
pearls: Recruit the NIV lead consultant and nurse; they own the chart.
Link the box to the existing Trust TEP form rather than creating a new one.
Audit the same episodes for time to NIV; it shows the plan does not slow treatment.
Keep plan completion as a standing item at NIV morbidity and mortality meetings.

pitfalls: Gases taken during a move between wards are missed → search the analyser for all gases on that patient, not the notes.
The NIV start time is not recorded → use the first recorded ventilator settings time and keep the rule for both cycles.
Patients moved to ICU early are counted twice → include only the ward NIV episode.
Nurses cannot take arterial samples → agree who takes the 2-hour gas out of hours before switching on the task.
pearls: Recruit the blood gas analyser point-of-care lead; the analyser export gives exact times.
Report the secondary 30-minute review to show why the gas matters.
Add the 2-hour gas to the NIV handover sheet.
Re-audit after the next junior doctor rotation to check it holds.

pitfalls: Weekend rota has no NIV-trained consultant → agree which consultants count before cycle 1 and report weekends separately.
Reviews by phone are not documented → count only a written review, and say so early.
Consultants feel judged on individual performance → present results by day and time, not by name.
Episodes starting in the evening skew the result → report median hours as well as the rate.
pearls: Recruit the respiratory clinical director; the fix is a rota issue.
Start with the list the NIV nurses already keep.
Show that most breaches cluster at weekends; it makes the case for a named weekend reviewer.
Keep the 14-hour figure on the NIV dashboard after the audit ends.

pitfalls: Old spirometry sits in GP records you cannot see → check the summary care record and ask one local practice to confirm a sample.
Patients are too unwell for spirometry soon after discharge → accept a request timed for 6–8 weeks after recovery.
The lung function lab worries about capacity → agree numbers with them before the change.
Requests are made but never done → record completion at 3 months as a secondary check.
pearls: Recruit the respiratory physiologist lead; they can tell you who has had spirometry in seconds.
Use the NACAP case list if your hospital submits; it saves coding searches.
Include a line in the discharge summary so the GP knows why spirometry matters.
Hand the bundle step to the COPD specialist nurses so it outlasts the audit team.

pitfalls: Referrals are made by the pulmonary rehabilitation team itself after discharge → check their log, not only the notes.
Patients declining are counted as fails → record documented declines as a pass, as agreed before cycle 1.
The rehabilitation service cannot enrol more people quickly → warn them and measure 30-day enrolment separately.
Non-respiratory wards miss the bundle → report results by discharging team.
pearls: Recruit the pulmonary rehabilitation coordinator; they know who was referred.
Ask patients' preference for venue at referral; it lifts uptake.
Use the NACAP data if your hospital submits.
Give the COPD nurses ownership of the bundle item after the audit.

pitfalls: ED discharges have no discharge summary → check the ED letter to the GP and count it only if it asks for review.
'Two working days' is miscounted over weekends → define working days before cycle 1 and keep the rule.
Practices may not act on an electronic task → agree the route with two local practices first.
Patients told to book themselves may not → record how it was arranged so the change can target it.
pearls: Recruit a respiratory nurse and an ED consultant; most asthma attacks leave from ED.
Pair the field with the written asthma action plan to keep discharge simple.
Ask a local GP to confirm a sample of appointments actually happened.
Put the field in the ED template as well as the ward template.

pitfalls: Wells score time is missing → use the CTPA request time as the start and keep it for both cycles.
Radiologists may resist an extra question on the request → keep it to one tick box and agree it with the radiology lead first.
Bleeding-risk patients are counted as fails → count a documented contraindication as a pass.
Scans done within the hour inflate the denominator → exclude them as the standard only applies when imaging is delayed.
pearls: Recruit a radiology registrar; RIS gives request and scan times in one export.
Agree the 1-hour definition of 'immediately' with ED and radiology before cycle 1.
Record whether PE was confirmed; untreated confirmed PE makes a strong case.
Keep the request question after the audit; it costs nothing.

pitfalls: Aspirations done on the ward leave no procedure note → find them from the laboratory pleural fluid list.
Radiology site-marking is counted as ultrasound use → agree before cycle 1 that only bedside ultrasound counts.
Out-of-hours procedures have no trained operator → report in-hours and out-of-hours separately.
Operators feel policed → present by location and time, not by name.
pearls: Recruit the pleural lead and the chest drain safety lead.
Check where the ultrasound machines are and who can use them before cycle 1.
Record complications; they make the case for the pleural list.
Keep a simple procedure log in the pleural room so the next audit takes minutes.

pitfalls: Paper checklists are lost after scanning → check scanned notes and the procedure log.
The post-procedure section is skipped when the operator leaves → make the post-check part of the nursing handover.
Aspirations on the ward are missed → use the laboratory pleural fluid list to find them.
Staff see it as box-ticking → share local pleural incidents to show why it matters.
pearls: Recruit the Trust NatSSIPs lead; they may already have the EPR form.
Agree what 'complete' means (all fields, signed) before cycle 1.
Put blank LocSSIPs in every chest drain pack while the EPR build is made.
Report procedure-room and ward results separately; wards usually lag.

pitfalls: Small effusions on X-ray are not truly eligible → record ultrasound depth and exclude effusions under 2 cm.
Clock start is disputed → use the first imaging report time in both cycles.
Weekend sampling depends on who can scan → report weekend and weekday results separately.
Numbers are small → extend the look-back period rather than lower the sample.
pearls: Recruit the pleural lead and a radiologist to run the report search.
Record pleural infection confirmed; it shows the yield of prompt sampling.
Link to the pleural list or ultrasound audit if run in the same year.
Keep the proforma step after the audit; it takes seconds.

pitfalls: Previous episodes at other hospitals are missed → ask about and search clinic letters for past pneumothorax.
Numbers are small → use a 12–24 month look-back and allow 6 months before re-audit.
Surgeons may not accept some referrals → count the offer as the pass, and record the surgical outcome separately.
Patients may decline surgery → count a documented informed decline as a pass.
pearls: Recruit a thoracic surgical registrar from the regional centre.
Agree the recurrence definition (second ipsilateral or first contralateral) before cycle 1.
Put the prompt in both the ED and respiratory discharge templates.
Add the prompt to the first respiratory clinic letter template as a safety net.

pitfalls: Falls not reported on the incident system are missed → cross-check against the falls prevention nurse's ward log.
Assessment done but filed outside the falls section of the EPR so it is missed on audit → agree one place to file it before cycle 1.
Small numbers on quieter wards → pool data across a division for 3 months.
Staff turnover between cycles loses the new habit → build the prompt into the incident-reporting software rather than relying on memory.
pearls: Recruit the falls prevention lead or matron as audit sponsor before cycle 1.
Agree with IT which EPR screen counts as 'the assessment' before collecting data.
Feed back ward-level results, not just a trust average, so staff see their own practice.
Re-audit on the same wards to see if the change has stuck after staff rotate.

pitfalls: Test omitted because staff feel too busy after an acute fall → make it part of the same set of post-fall observations, not a separate task.
Manual sphygmomanometer BP takes longer than automated → supply automated cuffs suitable for postural readings on falls-prone wards.
Definition of 'postural drop' varies between staff → print the numeric threshold on the chart.
Patient too unwell to stand → record the reason rather than leaving the field blank, so this is distinguished from omission.
pearls: Train healthcare assistants to do the test as part of routine falls observations.
Use the same chart used for the sepsis/NEWS2 observations so it is not a duplicate task.
Ask the falls nurse specialist to spot-check technique early in cycle 1.
Report both completion rate and the proportion found positive, to show the test finds real problems.

pitfalls: Examination done verbally at the bedside but not written up → give the examiner a one-line documentation prompt on the incident form.
Out-of-hours falls delay review → agree an explicit maximum time in the post-fall protocol and audit against it.
Small numbers if only one ward is sampled → pool falls across a division.
Definition of 'medical examination' disputed between cycles → fix the definition (doctor or ANP, hands-on assessment) before cycle 1.
pearls: Get sign-off on the post-fall protocol's time target from the on-call medical team before starting.
Use the falls incident form as the single place to record the examination, so nothing is duplicated.
Share results by specialty, since surgical and medical wards may have different cover patterns.
Keep the same protocol time target across cycles so the re-audit is a fair comparison.

pitfalls: Small numbers because qualifying falls are uncommon → extend the sampling period to 6 months.
Staff move the patient safely but do not write down the method → add a tick-list rather than free text.
Night-shift falls are less well documented → check the sample includes out-of-hours events.
Disagreement on what counts as 'signs of fracture' between cycles → use the same fixed list of signs both times.
pearls: Involve the moving and handling lead in designing the tick-list before cycle 1.
Use the same incident form used for the medical-examination audit, adding one field rather than a new form.
Share near-miss learning (e.g. hoists not available out of hours) at the safety huddle.
Keep the list of qualifying signs identical at re-audit.

pitfalls: Insertion documented in more than one place (drug chart, nursing notes, catheter care plan) so data are missed → agree one location before cycle 1.
Junior staff insert catheters out of hours without full documentation → include out-of-hours induction on the new form.
Retrospective completion after the audit is announced (Hawthorne effect) → sample unannounced and include very recent insertions.
Small numbers on low-catheterisation wards → combine several wards or extend the period.
pearls: Use a catheter passport that travels with the patient so the record is easy to find.
Involve the IPC nurse specialist in designing the mandatory fields.
Link completion of the form to catheter care plan initiation so it becomes routine, not extra work.
Re-audit the same wards after staff turnover to check the habit has stuck.

pitfalls: Review done verbally at handover but not written down → make the prompt part of the electronic care round, not a separate task.
Definition of 'no longer needed' varies by staff member → print the accepted indications list on the prompt.
Weekend and night reviews are less complete → include all days of the week in the sample, not just weekdays.
Reviewing nurse defers the decision to the ward round doctor and neither documents it → make either professional's entry count, but require one of them daily.
pearls: Base the accepted-indications list on a recognised tool (e.g. HOUDINI criteria) agreed with urology and microbiology.
Put the prompt in the same screen as other daily care bundle items (mouth care, pressure area care) so it is one round, not several.
Track catheter days per 1000 bed days alongside the audit as a balancing measure.
Re-audit on the same wards to check the daily habit survives a change of ward manager.

pitfalls: Observation itself changes behaviour on the day (Hawthorne effect) → do unannounced spot-checks, not a scheduled walkround.
Bag position changes when a patient mobilises → record the position as found, not after adjustment by the auditor.
Equipment shortage (no bag-hangers) undermines the fix → confirm supply before cycle 1.
Staff feel 'checked up on' → frame the audit as a safety check, not a performance review, and share results anonymously by ward.
pearls: Combine the spot-check with an existing safety walkround to avoid extra staff time.
Involve a student nurse or newly qualified nurse in doing the observations as a learning exercise.
Fix equipment gaps (bag-hangers, privacy covers) as part of the change, not just education.
Repeat the spot-check on different shifts to catch night-time practice.

pitfalls: Paper VIP charts are lost when patients move beds or wards → move scoring into the electronic record.
Scoring done but not at every shift as required → audit each shift separately rather than 'was it ever scored'.
Different staff interpret the VIP scale differently → include the VIP scale poster at every bed space.
Cannulas removed and re-sited are miscounted as one device → track by cannula episode, not by patient.
pearls: Put a VIP scale card on every drug trolley and at the bedside.
Make VIP scoring part of the same round as NEWS2 observations.
Recruit a link nurse for IV access on each ward to champion the change.
Track cannula-related bloodstream infections alongside the audit as a balancing measure.

pitfalls: Nurses wait for medical sign-off to remove a cannula, causing delay → confirm nurse-led removal is explicitly authorised in policy before cycle 1.
No alternative IV site available so removal is deferred appropriately → record this as a documented reason, not a failure.
Small numbers of qualifying events → extend the sampling period to 6 months.
VIP score under-recorded so events are missed (see the companion scoring-frequency audit) → run that audit alongside this one.
pearls: Run this audit alongside the VIP-scoring-frequency audit so both parts of the pathway are checked together.
Get sign-off from medicines management for nurse-led cannula removal before cycle 1.
Share phlebitis rates before and after the change as the outcome that matters to staff.
Keep the same 4-hour target at re-audit even if practice has improved, to show real change.

pitfalls: Auditors disturb the dressing to check it, risking dislodgement → train observers to inspect without touching.
Date obscured by tape or handwriting fades → use a printed date-label dressing pack.
Cannulas re-sited mid-stay are miscounted → record days since the current cannula's insertion, not the admission date.
Stock of the new dressing pack runs out → confirm procurement before cycle 1.
pearls: Combine this spot-check with the bag-position catheter audit as one 'devices' walkround.
Ask procurement to switch the default stocked dressing before starting the change.
Share photos (with consent, de-identified) of good and poor practice in ward teaching.
Repeat the walkround on different days of the week.

pitfalls: Central lines cared for on wards unfamiliar with the bundle miss checks → target ward education where lines are less common.
Check done but not documented → make it a mandatory electronic field, not a free-text note.
Small numbers of ward-based central lines → extend sampling to 6 months or include high-dependency areas.
Line removed early so fewer than 5 days of data are available → record only the days the line was actually in place.
pearls: Base the bundle on the trust's existing central line care bundle policy so nothing new is invented.
Involve the IV access/vascular access team in agreeing the mandatory fields.
Track central-line-associated bloodstream infection rates alongside the audit.
Re-audit after ward staff turnover to check the habit persists.

pitfalls: Review discussed verbally on the ward round but not written down → build the field into the ward round proforma, not a separate note.
Weekend ward rounds are less structured → include weekend days in the sample.
Definition of 'still needed' varies by team → agree a short accepted-indications list before cycle 1.
Line removed and a new one inserted is double-counted → track by line episode.
pearls: Pair this audit with the daily site/dressing check audit so both bundle elements are reviewed together.
Involve the consultant leading the ward round in championing the new field.
Track average central line dwell time as a balancing measure.
Feed results back promptly so the ward round team sees the impact of the change.

pitfalls: 4AT done but recorded outside the structured field, so it is missed → make one electronic field the single source of truth.
Staff confuse the 4AT with a full cognitive assessment (e.g. AMT4) → provide a laminated 4AT card at the bedside.
Busy admission units skip the 4AT under time pressure → make it part of the same screen as NEWS2 and falls risk, not an extra form.
Patients admitted out of hours are under-assessed → include night admissions in the sample.
pearls: Recruit the dementia/delirium specialist nurse to champion the mandatory field before cycle 1.
Provide short 4AT training at induction for all new admission-unit staff.
Report results separately for day and night admissions to find where the gap is.
Re-audit the same admission units after 6 months to check the mandatory field has bedded in.

pitfalls: A positive 4AT is scored but no one is notified → build an automatic alert rather than relying on the nurse to escalate verbally.
Out-of-hours positive scores wait until the next ward round → define an explicit same-day standard covering evenings and weekends.
Action plan documented but generic and not individualised → audit the presence of a medication review as a specific component.
Repeat 4AT scores in the same admission are double-counted → count only the first qualifying score per admission.
pearls: Use the same delirium action-plan template already used elsewhere in the trust rather than creating a new one.
Ask pharmacy to flag deliriogenic medicines automatically when the alert fires.
Share turnaround times (score to review) as well as the pass rate.
Re-audit on the same wards to check the alert has not been switched off or ignored.

pitfalls: Risk factors assessed informally during clerking but not recorded in a structured way → use fixed tick boxes, not free text.
Cognitive impairment missed because no baseline is known → ask a family member or GP record as a source.
Overlap with the 4AT audit causes double data entry → combine both into one admission screen.
Busy admissions units under time pressure skip non-mandatory fields → make the fields mandatory to save the clerking.
pearls: Combine this with the 4AT-within-24-hours audit as one admission bundle to save duplicate data collection.
Train admitting doctors and nurses together so both understand why the risk factors matter.
Use collateral history (family, care home, GP letter) systematically to assess cognitive impairment.
Report the proportion found to have at least one risk factor as well as the completion rate.

pitfalls: Prevention measures are done (e.g. a clock provided) but not documented → build a simple tick-list into the care plan rather than free text.
Care plan copied forward without individualisation → spot-check for generic, unedited entries.
Staff shortages limit mobility-related interventions → record barriers as well as completion.
Risk-at-risk flag is not consistently set, so eligible patients are missed → link the flag to the CG103 risk-factor audit.
pearls: Link this audit to the risk-factor assessment audit so the whole pathway from risk to prevention is checked.
Involve occupational therapy and volunteers (e.g. befriending schemes) in delivering orientation measures.
Provide clocks, calendars and large-print signage as ward equipment, not something staff must find.
Track delirium incidence on the ward as an outcome measure alongside process compliance.

pitfalls: Oxygen started as an emergency without a formal prescription → build a retrospective prompt into the EPR for the next drug round.
Staff assume 94-98% by default and do not write it down → make the field mandatory rather than relying on convention.
COPD patients not flagged as at risk of hypercapnia get the wrong target → link the oxygen order to the COPD/respiratory diagnosis flag where one exists.
Target range not updated when a blood gas result changes the picture → audit whether the range is reviewed after each blood gas.
pearls: Provide an oxygen alert card for patients known to be at risk of hypercapnia, to travel with them between wards.
Train new doctors at induction on the two target ranges and when each applies.
Use the respiratory team as champions on wards with high oxygen use.
Report results separately for COPD/at-risk patients and other patients.

pitfalls: Staff unfamiliar with variable-rate insulin infusions delay stopping it → target training at wards that manage diabetic ketoacidosis and perioperative patients.
Event not reported so the episode is missed from the sample → cross-check glucose meter downloads for readings below 4.0 mmol/L against incident reports.
Infusion restarted too early before the hypo is fully treated → audit this as a separate, later step.
Small numbers of qualifying episodes → extend the sampling period to 6 months across several wards.
pearls: Run this audit alongside the existing repeat-glucose-check audit to give a fuller picture of the hypo pathway.
Put the JBDS algorithm card inside every hypo box so the stop-infusion step cannot be missed.
Involve the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse team in reviewing every qualifying episode.
Feed back individual episode learning at ward level, not only the aggregate percentage.

pitfalls: Staff give whatever sugary item is to hand rather than a measured 15-20g dose → stock a standard hypo box.
Treatment given but not documented in detail (just 'hypo treated') → add a structured field naming the treatment and estimated carbohydrate content.
Patients on a low-potassium or fluid-restricted diet given an unsuitable treatment → audit for this as a specific error type.
Under-reporting of hypo episodes overall → cross-check against glucose meter downloads.
pearls: Introduction of standard hypo boxes has been shown elsewhere to raise correctly-managed episodes substantially; cite this local evidence when presenting.
Ask the diabetes specialist nurse team to restock and check hypo boxes on a fixed schedule.
Provide a laminated JBDS algorithm card inside each hypo box.
Report the proportion of episodes needing more than the initial treatment, as a marker of undertreatment.

pitfalls: Drug rounds are organised by ward routine rather than individual medicine timing → flag time-critical medicines so they are given outside the standard round if needed.
Patient admitted without their usual medicines brought in from home, causing delay while a supply is found → audit whether self-administration or 'own drugs' policies are used.
Nil-by-mouth patients have no alternative route considered → include a dispersible or patch alternative in the ward's Parkinson's toolkit.
eMAR times are rounded to the nearest 15 or 30 minutes by the system, masking small delays → confirm the system records exact times before relying on it.
pearls: Identify every inpatient with Parkinson's disease at the daily board round so nursing staff know who needs time-critical dosing.
Provide a 'Parkinson's disease: time-critical medicines' alert sticker for the drug chart or bedside.
Involve the Parkinson's disease specialist nurse in reviewing every admission with the condition.
Audit the reasons for delay as well as the headline rate, to target the fix at the real cause.

pitfalls: Meal trays arrive before the drug round reaches the patient → realign the round or use a 'give with meal' nurse-led protocol.
Patients who miss meals (off the ward for a scan) have insulin given at the wrong time → audit whether these are flagged and rescheduled.
eMAR times are rounded, masking real delays → confirm exact-time recording before relying on the system.
Sliding-scale corrections are confused with meal-time bolus insulin in the data → record dose type clearly.
pearls: Involve catering and nursing together in redesigning meal/drug round timing.
Use ward pharmacists to spot-check timing accuracy weekly during the collection period.
Provide point-of-care glucose meters on the drug trolley so checks and dosing happen together.
Share results with the ward as 'doses on time' rather than only 'doses missed', to keep the message positive.

pitfalls: List order changes on the day so a fixed fasting instruction becomes inaccurate → use a rolling sip-til-send system tied to the actual call time.
Ward staff default to 'nil by mouth from midnight' out of habit → replace the printed instruction on the pre-op leaflet and drug chart.
Patients over-restrict themselves beyond what is prescribed → give clear written instructions on what and when they may drink.
Definition of 'induction time' varies by data source → use the anaesthetic chart time consistently.
pearls: Involve theatre coordinators in agreeing a realistic call-time process before cycle 1.
Use patient information leaflets that state the sip-til-send instructions clearly.
Track cancellations and delays as a balancing measure to show the change has not caused new problems.
Re-audit after a full list cycle (including list re-ordering on the day) to test robustness.

pitfalls: Confused or unconscious patients cannot confirm their own identity → define the two-staff-member check as the alternative in the protocol.
Bedside check rushed when a unit is urgently needed → build the check into the electronic unit-release process so it cannot be bypassed.
Checklist completed on paper but filed separately from the prescription → keep it with the transfusion record.
100% target may feel unrealistic to staff → frame this explicitly as a zero-tolerance patient-identification safety step, distinct from other, more negotiable targets.
pearls: Involve the hospital transfusion practitioner in designing and auditing the checklist.
Use electronic bedside scanning where available, since it makes the check harder to skip.
Report any near-misses found during the audit directly to the transfusion committee, not just the percentage.
Re-audit unannounced, since a scheduled re-audit may prompt a temporary improvement.

pitfalls: Unit check and patient check are recorded as a single tick, hiding which part was actually done → separate them on the form.
Expired units are occasionally still in fridge stock → report any near-misses found to the blood bank immediately.
Staff assume the laboratory has already checked everything → reinforce that the bedside check is an independent final safeguard.
Rushed urgent transfusions skip the documented check → provide a rapid but complete checklist version for emergencies.
pearls: Combine with the patient-identification audit as one transfusion safety audit, reported as two separate results.
Use the hospital transfusion practitioner's existing spot-check programme as a data source where one exists.
Report any discrepancies found as a serious incident review trigger, not just an audit finding.
Keep the checklist short so it is actually used under time pressure.

pitfalls: Hand-written bands have transcription errors → move to printed bands generated from the EPR.
Bands not replaced after a name or NHS number correction on the EPR → add a prompt to reprint the band whenever demographics are amended.
Auditors themselves misread small print → use a standard checklist and, where possible, compare to a second printed source (e.g. wristband label copy).
Sensitive to Hawthorne effect if staff know the audit is happening → do the spot-check without prior ward announcement.
pearls: Combine this with the transfusion identification audit so both use the same observation visit.
Involve ward clerks, who often apply bands on admission, in the change process.
Feed back errors found immediately to the ward so they can be corrected on the spot, in addition to the aggregate report.
Repeat the spot-check on different wards and shifts to get a representative picture.

pitfalls: Allergy identified after the white band is already applied and the band is not changed → add an automatic reminder when a new allergy is documented.
Red bands not stocked on the ward when needed → confirm supply as part of the change.
Allergy status disputed or uncertain (e.g. intolerance vs true allergy) → use the trust's existing allergy documentation policy to decide what counts.
Patients transferred from another ward keep an old band that was never updated → include a band check in the transfer checklist.
pearls: Combine this spot-check with the general identity band accuracy audit.
Involve pharmacy in reviewing any mismatches found, since these are medicines safety incidents.
Make sure red bands are as freely available as white ones on every ward.
Report mismatches found as safety learning at ward level, not just an aggregate percentage.

pitfalls: Small numbers, since most patients do wear a band → extend the audit period or pool wards with higher rates of confusion/mental health needs.
Staff avoid raising the issue with the patient again once refused once → make re-attempting the explanation part of the daily care plan review.
Photograph consent process is unfamiliar to staff → provide a simple one-page guide at the nursing station.
Confusion between 'refused' and 'clinically unable' (e.g. skin condition) is not distinguished → record the specific reason, not just 'no band'.
pearls: Focus data collection on wards with higher numbers of patients with dementia, delirium or acute mental health needs.
Involve the safeguarding and dementia teams in designing the alternative-identification process.
Review with patients and carers, where possible, whether the alternative process felt respectful.
Re-audit on the same wards after staff turnover to check the process has bedded in.

pitfalls: Transfer checklists are completed retrospectively rather than at the time → make the identity check the first item, ahead of clinical handover.
Verbal handover replaces the written checklist → require the checklist to travel with the patient's notes.
Bed pressures lead to rushed transfers where the checklist is skipped → audit out-of-hours and high-occupancy periods specifically.
Discrepancies found are not escalated → add a clear 'what to do if a discrepancy is found' step to the checklist.
pearls: Use the same transfer checklist already required for other information (e.g. VTE status, allergies) so this is one extra line, not a new form.
Train bed managers and site teams on the importance of this final identity check.
Report any discrepancies found as safety learning, in addition to the completion rate.
Re-audit at a different time of year to check winter bed-pressure periods are not worse.

pitfalls: Bed rails put up as a default without individual assessment → make the assessment a prerequisite in the EPR order.
Risk assessment done once on admission and not reviewed when the patient's condition changes → audit whether it is reviewed after any relevant change.
Staff underestimate entrapment risk because they see bed rails as routine → include Never Event learning in ward teaching.
Assessment completed but not accessible to night staff → keep it in a single, easy-to-find EPR location.
pearls: Use the MHRA's example adult entrapment risk assessment checklist as the basis for the EPR form.
Involve the moving and handling/tissue viability team in reviewing findings.
Report any Never Event near-misses found during the audit immediately through the incident system.
Repeat the spot-check on wards with higher rates of confusion or frailty.

pitfalls: Explanation given verbally but not recorded → add a specific field rather than relying on general nursing notes.
Patients who lack capacity are not covered by a best-interests decision → link the field to the trust's Mental Capacity Act documentation.
Family not contactable at the time bed rails are first used → record this and require follow-up documentation once contact is made.
Staff see this as extra paperwork → combine it with the risk assessment form so it is one document, not two.
pearls: Combine this audit with the risk-assessment-before-use audit as one bed rails safety audit.
Provide a simple patient/family information leaflet on bed rails to support the conversation.
Involve the mental capacity/best interests lead where patients lack capacity.
Share good-practice examples of clear documentation at ward teaching sessions.

pitfalls: Mattress replaced (e.g. for pressure relief) without repeating the bed rail check → link mattress ordering to an automatic bed rail re-check prompt.
Checks become a tick-box exercise without real inspection → include a photo-based training aid on what to look for.
Night shift checks are less thorough → include night shifts explicitly in the sample.
Staff unfamiliar with entrapment zones → provide the MHRA entrapment-area diagram at the nursing station.
pearls: Combine with other intentional rounding items (pressure area care, hydration) so it is one round.
Use the MHRA entrapment risk-area diagram for staff training.
Involve estates/equipment teams when a mismatched bed and mattress combination is found.
Report any hazards found immediately, not only in the aggregate audit result.

pitfalls: Staff are unsure whether a concern meets the referral threshold and delay while seeking advice → provide a same-day advice line staffed by the trust safeguarding team.
Concerns identified out of hours wait until the next working day → confirm an out-of-hours referral route exists and is used.
Small numbers of qualifying concerns on general wards → extend sampling to 6 months or pool several wards.
Referral made verbally to a colleague but not formally submitted → audit only formal referrals recorded in the safeguarding log.
pearls: Work with the trust safeguarding adults lead to define what counts as 'identified' versus 'referred'.
Provide a laminated safeguarding referral pathway card on every ward.
Report both the same-day rate and the reasons for any delay found.
Re-audit after staff safeguarding training to see if the change has had an effect.

pitfalls: Rapid tranquillisation episodes are uncommon on general wards, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period to 6-12 months across the whole trust.
Standard NEWS2 charts do not capture hydration or consciousness in the way needed → use a dedicated chart rather than the routine observation chart.
Staff are focused on managing the acute behavioural disturbance and monitoring is deprioritised → assign a named member of staff to monitoring at the time the drug is given.
Episodes are not all captured on the incident system → cross-check against pharmacy records of parenteral sedatives given.
pearls: Involve the mental health liaison team, who are often called to these episodes on general wards.
Use a pre-printed sticker or EPR order set that starts the monitoring schedule automatically.
Review every episode with a debrief involving the nurse in charge, not only the aggregate percentage.
Track any adverse events (oversedation, respiratory depression) alongside the audit as an outcome measure.

pitfalls: Incident forms focus on what happened rather than why that level of restriction was chosen → add specific fields rather than free text alone.
Staff under time pressure after an incident complete the form minimally → allow the form to be completed in two stages (immediate facts, then reflection within 24 hours).
Small numbers of restraint episodes on general wards → extend the sampling period.
Different staff have different thresholds for what counts as 'least restrictive' → provide training and examples.
pearls: Run this alongside the existing post-incident debrief audit so the whole NG10 documentation standard is reviewed together.
Involve service user representatives in reviewing what good documentation looks like.
Use restrictive intervention reduction programme data (already required by NG10) as a source of episodes.
Share themes from the reasons documented, not just the completion rate, to guide training.

pitfalls: Mouth care assessment seen as a low priority compared with other admission tasks → make it part of the same mandatory admission bundle as pressure ulcer and falls risk assessment.
Staff lack confidence assessing the mouth without dental training → provide short Mouth Care Matters training and a simple visual guide.
Assessment done but not reviewed weekly as required → track weekly review as a separate, later measure.
Patients with dentures or dysphagia need a modified approach not captured by a simple tool → add a free-text note field for these cases.
pearls: Use the trust's existing Mouth Care Matters-based assessment tool rather than creating a new one.
Provide a basic mouth care kit at every bedside so assessment leads straight into action.
Involve speech and language therapy for patients with dysphagia identified through the assessment.
Report results alongside pressure ulcer and falls assessment rates, since all three are part of the same admission bundle.

pitfalls: Mouth care given but not recorded → build recording into the same electronic round as repositioning and hydration.
Staff shortages mean mouth care is deprioritised against other tasks → make it an explicit, named item on the intentional rounding chart rather than assumed.
Patients who are nil by mouth are wrongly assumed not to need mouth care → clarify that NBM patients need mouth care even more, not less.
Reduced consciousness or intubated patients need a different technique not distinguished on a simple chart → add a note field for special techniques used.
pearls: Stock basic mouth care kits (sponge sticks, non-foaming toothpaste) on every bed bay.
Train healthcare assistants specifically, since they often deliver most mouth care.
Combine this audit with the mouth care assessment audit to review the full pathway.
Report results by ward, since dependency levels vary a great deal between specialties.

pitfalls: Reason entered as vague free text ('N/A') that does not explain the cause → use a fixed drop-down list of reason categories.
Staff do not know which medicines on the chart are time-critical → flag them visually on the eMAR.
Doses omitted overnight are under-documented due to lower staffing → include night shifts in the sample.
Reason coding varies between wards using paper versus electronic charts → restrict the audit to wards on the same eMAR system for consistency.
pearls: Agree the trust's time-critical medicines list with pharmacy before starting data collection.
Use the coded reasons to run a monthly pharmacy-led review of recurring causes.
Pair this audit with the specific Parkinson's and insulin timing audits to build a full picture.
Feed back common reasons (e.g. 'medicine not available') to procurement or ward stock processes.

pitfalls: Communication delay between theatres and the ward means the ward is unaware of the cancellation → use a direct phone call, not just an electronic list update.
Patient still due to be rescheduled later the same day so remains fasted appropriately → record this as a valid reason, not a failure.
Cancellations late in the day are under-recorded because staff focus on other tasks → include all times of day in the sample.
No consistent record of when the patient was actually told → agree a single point of documentation (nursing notes) for this time.
pearls: Give the theatre coordinator a one-line script to use when phoning the ward.
Track patient-reported experience of cancellation alongside the audit as a balancing measure.
Share cancellation and fasting-related complaints with the theatres team to reinforce the case for change.
Re-audit during a busy winter period to test the process under pressure.

pitfalls: Urgent situations mean consultation happens after, not before, the intervention → accept and record retrospective consultation as long as it is documented promptly.
No carer or family member is contactable → record this explicitly rather than leaving the field blank.
Capacity assessment itself is not documented, making the population hard to define → run this audit alongside a capacity-documentation check.
Staff conflate 'informing' a family member after the event with 'involving' them in the decision → clarify the distinction in training.
pearls: Link this audit to the trust's existing Mental Capacity Act training programme.
Involve the safeguarding and mental capacity leads in reviewing findings.
Provide a quick-reference card on when and how to contact carers out of hours.
Report findings alongside the least-restrictive-intervention audit for a fuller picture of NG10 compliance.

pitfalls: Glucose checks recorded on a separate paper chart not linked to the EPR infusion order → move monitoring into the same electronic system as the infusion.
Checks clustered together after a gap rather than genuinely hourly → measure the longest gap, not just the total number of checks.
Ward staffing pressure causes delays overnight → include night hours specifically in the sample.
Infusion stopped and restarted multiple times, complicating the 12-hour window → record only the first continuous run.
pearls: Use networked glucose meters that time-stamp readings automatically to reduce data collection effort.
Involve the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse team in reviewing outlying cases.
Track hypoglycaemia and severe hyperglycaemia rates on infusions as an outcome measure alongside monitoring frequency.
Re-audit on wards less familiar with insulin infusions, such as surgical wards, separately from specialist diabetes wards.

pitfalls: Immunisation history from other countries is often unavailable → record as 'unknown after checking' rather than assuming fully vaccinated, and offer catch-up unless clear written evidence of 2 doses exists.
Reception staff may not prompt the MMR question at registration → build it into the mandatory new-patient questionnaire, not a free-text box.
Small numbers of eligible unvaccinated adults in some practices → extend the sampling window to 6 months if fewer than 40 new registrations are found.
Staff may worry about vaccine hesitancy conversations taking appointment time → agree a short scripted offer and a nurse-led catch-up clinic slot before cycle 1.
Gains fade once the new-patient template reverts to a free-text field after a system upgrade → re-check the template build after any EPR update.
pearls: Recruit the practice nurse who runs new-patient checks as the change champion before cycle 1.
Agree the catch-up MMR offer script and consent process with the whole team before starting data collection.
Use the same registration list report each cycle so the sample is reproducible.
Link the audit to the practice's outbreak-preparedness discussion to keep it a clinical priority after the lead rotates.

pitfalls: Age-based call/recall systems will not flag immunosuppressed patients under 50 or 60 → build a separate immunosuppression-register search rather than relying on the age search.
Defining 'severely immunosuppressed' consistently is hard → agree the practice's operational definition (drug list and doses) with a GP before starting.
Small numbers per practice → consider a PCN-level audit pooling several practices.
Clinicians may be unsure about timing relative to chemotherapy cycles → agree a simple rule (for example, avoid the week of chemotherapy) with a specialist in advance.
The immunosuppression register itself may be incomplete → cross-check against recent hospital letters and repeat prescriptions for biologics or high-dose steroids.
pearls: Ask the practice pharmacist to build and run the register cross-reference; they already handle DMARD/biologic searches.
Agree with hospital specialists a simple safe-timing rule for vaccination around treatment before cycle 1.
Use the same immunosuppression register definition at re-audit so the sample is comparable.
Keep the monthly search running after the audit team rotates by assigning it a named permanent owner, not an individual GP.

pitfalls: Risk-group coding is often incomplete or inconsistent between clinicians → agree a fixed code list with the coding lead before starting.
Diagnoses made in secondary care may not be coded in primary care promptly → include a check of recent discharge summaries and clinic letters in the search.
Patients may decline vaccination → count a documented, informed decline as meeting the standard.
The 3-month window may be too tight for patients seen infrequently → confirm the window with the team before cycle 1 rather than changing it after seeing the results.
Alert fatigue if too many pop-ups are added to the EPR → restrict the new alert to the specific risk-group codes being audited.
pearls: Ask the practice's data quality lead to build the risk-group code search; it can be reused for other opportunistic vaccination audits.
Agree with the nursing team who owns the task list generated by the alert before go-live.
Use the same code list at re-audit to keep the sample comparable.
Fold the alert into the standard new-diagnosis workflow so it survives staff turnover.

pitfalls: Immunisation records may show the vaccine name but not clearly flag it as needing a 5-year recall → use a dedicated recall date field rather than relying on staff remembering the rule.
Patients may have moved practices since their first dose, losing the vaccination date → request records from PCSE/previous practice where the date is missing.
Small numbers at individual practice level → combine data across a PCN if needed to reach 30-40 cases.
Confusing PPV23 with the routine over-65 dose → clarify in the template that this audit is only about the 5-yearly at-risk revaccination.
Recall lists not reviewed once built → assign a named administrator to run and act on the quarterly search.
pearls: Ask the practice's long-term conditions nurse to lead, since they already run the asplenia/CKD annual review.
Agree the exact due-date calculation (last dose + 5 years) with the whole team before cycle 1.
Use the same register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Hand the quarterly search to the practice's routine search rota so it continues after the lead moves on.

pitfalls: Smoking status may be out of date → include a rule to re-check status if it has not been updated in 12 months.
Staff may feel repeated advice annoys patients → agree brief, non-judgemental wording in advance, as NICE recommends.
Recording bias: 'discussed' may be ticked without a genuine conversation → spot-check a sample of consultation free text alongside the coded box.
Referral pathways to external stop-smoking services vary by area and may be confusing → print the local referral route on the consultation template before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade once the prompt becomes routine and is dismissed automatically → review click-through rates at re-audit, not just referral numbers.
pearls: Recruit the practice's health promotion or long-term conditions lead to champion the template change.
Agree the referral pathway and paperwork with the local stop-smoking service before cycle 1.
Keep the same coded smoking-status search for both cycles so results are comparable.
Report referral numbers back to reception and nursing staff regularly to sustain motivation after the lead moves on.

pitfalls: Screening and brief intervention may both be ticked as done without a genuine 5-15 minute conversation → spot-check free-text notes against the coded box.
Appointment time pressure may push staff to skip the intervention → build a 10-minute brief-intervention slot into nurse or HCA clinics.
Patients scoring in the possible-dependence range need a different pathway (full assessment, not brief intervention) → exclude them from this audit and route separately.
Staff training in FRAMES-based brief advice varies → agree and circulate one resource before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade if the template field becomes a routine tick-box → review free-text quality at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit a practice nurse or HCA trained in alcohol brief intervention to champion the change.
Agree the FRAMES-based resource and script with the whole team before starting data collection.
Use the same AUDIT/AUDIT-C threshold definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Keep the mandatory template field live after the audit team rotates by building it into new-starter induction.

pitfalls: Vaccination may be delivered by the maternity unit rather than the GP practice, so records can be incomplete in the GP system → cross-check with the hand-held maternity notes or shared care record.
Some women decline vaccination → record a documented, informed decline as distinct from a missed offer.
Late bookers may reach 20 weeks with little time before 32 weeks → flag these women for an earlier offer at booking.
Coding of pregnancy stage may be inconsistent → agree a standard gestation-recording method before starting.
Improvement may not persist if midwifery and GP records are not integrated → confirm information-sharing arrangements with the maternity unit before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the practice's maternity liaison midwife or lead GP to champion the reminder task.
Agree with the local maternity unit how vaccination given there will be recorded back in the GP system.
Use the same maternity register extraction method at re-audit.
Keep the reminder task linked to the booking bloods step so it continues automatically after the audit lead moves on.

pitfalls: The non-responder list may not be checked regularly if no one owns the task → name a specific administrator and add it to their job plan before cycle 1.
Opportunistic flags may be added but never actioned at the next visit → audit whether the flag led to a discussion, not just whether it was added.
Patients who have valid reasons for non-attendance (for example, no cervix, pregnancy) should be excluded or ceased, not repeatedly chased → build a clear ceasing pathway.
Data protection and consent must be respected for phone calls → confirm the practice's telephone contact policy before starting.
Improvement may fade if the CSMS list is not checked after the administrator changes role → document the process in a standard operating procedure.
pearls: Recruit the practice's screening administrator as the audit lead, since they already access CSMS.
Agree a short call script and letter template addressing common barriers (fear, embarrassment, cultural sensitivity) before cycle 1.
Use the same CSMS extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Write the monthly review into a standard operating procedure so it survives staff changes.

pitfalls: DNA management is often left to individual staff discretion → write a single agreed local DNA policy before cycle 1.
Contact details may be out of date, especially for less engaged groups → verify phone numbers at the point of first invitation.
Practices may deprioritise Health Checks against same-day clinical demand → protect specific appointment slots for the programme.
Equity: some groups (deprived, hard-to-reach) DNA more often and need tailored, not just repeated, invitations → review DNA rates by deprivation decile if data allow.
Improvement may fade once the automatic rule is switched off after a system change → check the rule is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the healthcare assistant or nurse who runs the Health Check clinic to lead the audit.
Agree the second-contact method and script with reception before cycle 1.
Use the same invitation log extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report DNA and re-invitation rates to the practice manager regularly to keep the recall rule prioritised after the lead rotates.

pitfalls: Late-night or high-volume receptions create time pressure that can push assessment after cell allocation → agree an escalation process for surge nights before cycle 1.
Custody and healthcare IT systems may not talk to each other, making the sequencing hard to verify → use manual timestamp checks if systems are not linked.
Staff may complete the assessment but backdate or forget to timestamp it → audit against the reception log time, not just presence of a record.
Reduced staffing at weekends and bank holidays → review results by day of week to check for a pattern.
The IT dependency change needs governor and healthcare provider sign-off together → secure both before cycle 1, not after.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's head of residence together, since this crosses healthcare and custodial systems.
Agree the IT change with both the healthcare records supplier and the prison establishment before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at the joint health and justice partnership board so the change survives staff and contract rotation.

pitfalls: Staff shortages on the nursing team can push second-stage assessments beyond 7 days → review staffing rotas alongside the audit results.
People released or transferred within 7 days will not have a completed second-stage assessment for a valid reason → exclude them rather than counting as a failure.
IT worklists may not be checked if not part of the daily routine → build the check into the nursing handover, not a separate report.
Assessment quality may drop if teams rush to hit the 7-day target → spot-check a sample of second-stage assessments for completeness alongside timeliness.
Improvement may fade if the worklist task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm it is still functioning at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's senior nurse for reception healthcare as the audit lead.
Agree the worklist design with the nursing team before cycle 1 so it fits their existing handover process.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Review the worklist task list at the weekly clinical governance meeting so it stays visible after the audit team changes.

pitfalls: Community medication lists brought in by the person may be incomplete or unverifiable → agree a process for contacting the community pharmacy or GP the same day.
Critical medicines (for example, anticonvulsants, insulin, opioid substitution therapy) need faster action than routine ones → prioritise these using the NG57 table 2 critical medicines list.
Reception nights with high volume may overwhelm the pharmacist worklist → agree an escalation and cover plan before cycle 1.
Paper-based medicine charts can be lost between reception and the wing → track the chart alongside the person, not as a separate document.
Improvement may fade if the electronic referral is bypassed during IT downtime → have a clear paper backup process and check it is used correctly at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and reception nurse lead jointly, since this spans both roles.
Agree escalation routes for out-of-hours prescribing before starting data collection.
Use the same critical-medicines definition (NG57 table 2) at re-audit.
Report near misses as well as full audit results to keep the pathway prioritised after the lead rotates.

pitfalls: Community pharmacies or prescribers may be unreachable out of hours or at weekends → agree an escalation and interim-dose protocol with clinical leadership before cycle 1.
Self-reported doses may be inaccurate or exaggerated → always attempt independent confirmation before prescribing the full dose.
Reception at night or on Fridays increases delay risk → review results by day/time of reception.
Prescribers may be reluctant to prescribe without full confirmation, causing safe but slow practice → agree a documented interim bridging protocol for uncertain cases.
Improvement may fade if the confirmation pathway relies on one enthusiastic clinician → build it into the substance misuse team's standard operating procedure.
pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead clinician and the reception nurse team together.
Agree the interim bridging protocol and escalation contacts with the substance misuse service before cycle 1.
Use the same OST-reporting definition at re-audit.
Report near-miss delays as well as completed audits at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.

pitfalls: People may be transferred or released before results are back → build a handover process that follows the result, not just the person's location on the day of testing.
Opt-out testing still requires informed consent and cultural sensitivity → agree a standard explanation script before cycle 1.
Segregation or healthcare in-patient status can make results harder to deliver in person → include a specific check for these locations in the tracking flag.
Laboratory turnaround delays are outside the practice's control → report delays separately from delivery failures.
Improvement may fade if the electronic flag is closed prematurely → spot-check a sample of 'result given' entries against actual documented conversations.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse and NHS hepatitis lead jointly.
Agree the opt-out script and consent process with the whole reception team before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report testing and result-delivery rates to the health and justice partnership board so the pathway survives contract and staff changes.

pitfalls: Staff may assume HIV testing is only needed for people reporting risk factors, contrary to the opt-out approach recommended → make it a default with reasoned opt-out, not opt-in.
Stigma concerns may make some staff hesitant to raise the offer routinely → provide brief training and a standard script before cycle 1.
Reception time pressure can push non-mandatory items to be skipped → make the combined BBV block a required field before the assessment can be saved.
Repeat testing of people known to be already diagnosed wastes capacity → exclude them clearly in the template.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later made optional in an IT update → confirm the field remains mandatory at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse as the audit lead, combining this with the hepatitis B/C audit for efficiency.
Agree a brief non-stigmatising offer script with the whole reception team before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report the combined BBV testing rate at the health and justice partnership board to keep it prioritised after staff turnover.

pitfalls: TB screening and BBV testing are often commissioned and delivered by separate teams → agree a single combined pathway and blood-draw process before cycle 1.
Establishing whether a prison 'receives from high incidence areas' needs local public health input → confirm this with the local TB team before starting.
Support for continuing treatment after release is a precondition in the NICE recommendation → confirm community follow-up arrangements are in place before offering testing.
Substance misuse service attendance is often episodic → use the first contact in the audit period as the index event, not every subsequent contact.
Improvement may fade if the combined order set reverts to separate requests after an IT change → check it remains combined at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the substance misuse lead nurse and the multidisciplinary TB team jointly, since NICE requires their integration.
Confirm continuity-of-care arrangements for post-release treatment before cycle 1, as NICE specifies.
Use the same substance misuse service contact definition at re-audit.
Report combined testing rates at the joint TB/substance misuse governance meeting to keep the pathway prioritised after staff turnover.

pitfalls: TB screening may be recorded as part of the general health assessment without a separate timestamp → add a dedicated TB screening field with its own date/time.
Access to mobile X-ray or IGRA testing may be limited out of hours → agree local arrangements for weekend and night receptions before cycle 1.
People who decline screening should be recorded distinctly from those simply not yet screened → add a 'declined' option to avoid conflating the two.
High reception volumes on a single day can delay screening for later arrivals → review results by daily reception volume.
Improvement may fade if the countdown task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm the task list still functions at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the local multidisciplinary TB team liaison together.
Agree out-of-hours screening arrangements (for example, symptom screen with X-ray to follow) before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report the 48-hour completion rate at the multidisciplinary TB team meeting so it remains visible after the audit lead moves on.

pitfalls: Healthcare staffing levels may not allow attendance at every case review, especially out of hours → ensure the written/verbal contribution route is genuinely available as a fallback.
'Attendance' may be recorded loosely without confirming a genuine clinical contribution was made → audit the content of the contribution, not just a tick box.
ACCT and healthcare records sit on different IT systems in most establishments → agree a cross-referencing method before cycle 1.
Case reviews may be rescheduled at short notice, making healthcare attendance harder to plan → build early notification into the concern-form process, as the framework requires.
Improvement may fade if the notification step is seen as an add-on rather than mandatory → make it part of the ACCT case co-ordinator's checklist.
pearls: Recruit the safer custody lead and the prison's senior healthcare clinical lead jointly, since this crosses both services.
Agree the notification and escalation process with both teams before cycle 1.
Use the same ACCT/case review extraction method at re-audit.
Report results at the joint safer custody and healthcare governance meeting so the pathway survives staff turnover.

pitfalls: Short-notice releases (for example, following a court decision) leave little time to prepare medicines → build a same-day pharmacy fast-track process for unplanned releases (see NG57 1.7.15).
Controlled drugs and opioid substitution therapy need specific arrangements with community providers → confirm the community pharmacy handover process before cycle 1.
People released without a fixed address may struggle to access a community pharmacy → note this in the risk assessment rather than skipping the medicines supply.
FP10 prescriptions may not be dispensed promptly in the community → measure days supplied given directly where possible, not just the prescription being issued.
Improvement may fade if pharmacy staffing is reduced → review staffing alongside the audit results.
pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and resettlement/throughcare team jointly.
Agree the fast-track process for unplanned releases before cycle 1, as NG57 requires a contingency plan.
Use the same discharge record extraction method at re-audit.
Report results at the resettlement and medicines optimisation governance meetings so the checklist item survives contract or staff changes.

pitfalls: Reception staff have many competing priorities at first-stage assessment → make the smoking field mandatory rather than optional to prevent it being missed.
Withdrawal symptoms may be attributed to other causes if not specifically asked about → train reception staff to recognise and act on nicotine withdrawal.
NRT stock shortages can undermine same-day support → confirm supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Vaping status may not be captured separately from smoking, complicating the denominator → clarify the definition of 'current smoker' before starting.
Improvement may fade if NRT is only offered at reception and not continued on the wing → check continuation rates as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's smoke-free/stop-smoking coordinator jointly.
Agree the NRT order set and supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.
